title: A Telephone on the Hall Table
description: Return to a familiar landline telephone and the words for its handset, controls, and connection.
cardDescription: Return to a familiar landline telephone and the words for its handset, controls, and connection.
subtheme: A Telephone on the Hall Table
focus: The clues describe a traditional corded telephone rather than every modern phone. Some objects have several everyday names, so the definitions specify their parts and functions.
solvingTip: Look for whether the clue names a whole unit, a control, or a sound. Short calling words will help with the longer equipment names.
words: HANDSET
Telephone part held with both an earpiece and a mouthpiece
RECEIVER
Telephone term traditionally used for the part held to the ear
ROTARY
Describing a telephone dial that turns and returns
RINGER
Device in a telephone that sounds an incoming-call alert
HOOK
Telephone cradle switch, as in taking a phone off the ___
DIAL
Circular numbered control on an older telephone
CORD
Flexible cable joining a traditional handset to its base
NUMBER
Sequence of digits identifying a telephone connection
CALL
Attempt to reach someone by telephone
LINE
Connection carrying a conventional landline conversation
TONE
Steady sound heard before dialing on many phone systems
PHONE
Short everyday name for a telephone
SPEAK
To send words into the telephone's mouthpiece
LISTEN
To hear the other person's voice through the earpiece

answerNotes.HANDSET: A handset combines the parts held near the ear and mouth. It is distinct from the telephone base resting on the table.
answerNotes.RECEIVER: Receiver can mean the listening component or, informally, the handset. The wording here specifies its traditional listening role.
answerNotes.ROTARY: A rotary dial sends pulses as it returns. The word describes the mechanism rather than the sound of the bell.
answerNotes.RINGER: The ringer produces the alert. The voice heard during a call comes through the listening component instead.
answerNotes.HOOK: Off the hook refers to lifting the handset from its resting switch. It does not require a literal wall hook on every telephone.

title: A Familiar Film Camera
description: Look through the parts of a film camera, from the light-controlling opening to the place where the picture is composed.
cardDescription: Look through the parts of a film camera, from the light-controlling opening to the place where the picture is composed.
focus: The scene uses a film camera to make the vocabulary concrete. A shutter controls exposure time, an aperture is an opening, and a viewfinder helps compose the picture.
solvingTip: Use each part’s job to distinguish it. Making an image sharp, letting light in, and enlarging the view require different words.
words: CAMERA
Device used to record a photograph on film
SHUTTER
Camera mechanism that opens to admit light for an exposure
APERTURE
Adjustable opening controlling how much light enters a camera
VIEWFINDER
Camera viewing window used to compose a picture
FOCUS
Camera adjustment that makes the subject appear sharp
LENS
Optical assembly at the front of a camera
FILM
Light-sensitive strip loaded into a traditional camera
FRAME
One picture area on a roll of photographic film
FLASH
Brief burst of added light for a photograph
TRIPOD
Three-legged support used to steady a camera
ZOOM
To vary a lens's focal length for a wider or closer view
IMAGE
Picture formed by a camera's optical system
CASE
Protective container for carrying a camera
CAP
Removable protective cover for a camera lens

answerNotes.CAMERA: This scene concerns a film camera. Digital cameras share some parts but record the image differently.
answerNotes.SHUTTER: The shutter controls exposure duration. The aperture controls the size of the light-passing opening.
answerNotes.APERTURE: Aperture refers to the opening, not the time it remains exposed. Both aperture and shutter timing affect an exposure.
answerNotes.VIEWFINDER: A viewfinder helps frame the subject. Its view need not be identical in design across all camera types.
answerNotes.FOCUS: Focus concerns sharpness at the subject's distance. Zoom changes the lens's focal length rather than simply correcting focus.

title: The Home Sewing Machine
description: Recognize the moving parts and familiar materials of a household sewing machine.
cardDescription: Recognize the moving parts and familiar materials of a household sewing machine.
focus: The clues distinguish the lower thread supply, the operator’s control, and the parts that move fabric. Some familiar words have a specific mechanical meaning in this setting.
solvingTip: A clue may ask for a component, a material, or the result of sewing. Use that distinction to separate short words with several meanings.
words: BOBBIN
Small spool holding the lower thread in many sewing machines
PEDAL
Foot-operated control used to run many sewing machines
TENSION
Adjustment controlling how tightly sewing threads are held
DOG
Feed ___, toothed machine part that advances fabric
FOOT
Presser ___, part that holds fabric against the feeding mechanism
NEEDLE
Pointed machine part carrying thread through fabric
SPOOL
Cylinder holding the upper sewing thread
THREAD
Fine strand that forms a sewn stitch
STITCH
Single unit of sewing formed by the machine
FEED
To move fabric forward through the sewing mechanism
HEM
Folded and sewn finish at a fabric edge
SEAM
Line of stitching joining pieces of fabric
WHEEL
Round hand-operated part used to turn the machine mechanism
BELT
Flexible drive loop found on many older sewing machines

answerNotes.BOBBIN: The bobbin supplies the lower thread in a typical lockstitch machine. The upper thread comes from another spool.
answerNotes.PEDAL: A pedal is operated by the foot. It differs from the presser foot that rests on the fabric.
answerNotes.TENSION: Balanced thread tension helps form a suitable stitch. The word names a thread-control setting rather than speed.
answerNotes.DOG: Feed dogs move the fabric beneath the presser foot. Dog has a mechanical meaning in this phrase rather than naming an animal.
answerNotes.FOOT: The presser foot holds the work against the feed dogs. It is separate from the operator's foot pedal.

title: A Kitchen Timer and Clock
description: Compare a clock’s time-of-day display with a timer’s measured interval through familiar mechanical parts and sounds.
cardDescription: Compare a clock’s time-of-day display with a timer’s measured interval through familiar mechanical parts and sounds.
focus: A clock tells the time of day; a timer measures an interval. The clues use traditional dial and spring-driven mechanisms without assuming that every modern device contains those parts.
solvingTip: Watch whether the clue asks for a period, a moving component, or an alert. Those categories separate several short familiar words.
words: TIMER
Device that measures a chosen interval before giving an alert
SPRING
Coiled part storing energy in a wind-up mechanism
GEAR
Toothed wheel transferring motion inside a mechanical clock
HAND
Pointer moving around a traditional clock face
MINUTE
Time unit equal to sixty seconds
WIND
To turn a key or knob to store energy in a spring
DIAL
Numbered face read on an analog kitchen clock
ALARM
Audible signal announcing that a set time has arrived
SECOND
Time unit equal to one sixtieth of a minute
HOUR
Time unit equal to sixty minutes
CLOCK
Device displaying the time of day
BELL
Metal sounder used in some traditional kitchen timers
TICK
Short repeated sound associated with a mechanical clock
KNOB
Small turning control used to set a timer

answerNotes.TIMER: A timer measures elapsed time or counts down an interval. A clock generally displays the time of day.
answerNotes.SPRING: Winding a spring stores mechanical energy. Electronic timers do not necessarily contain this kind of drive.
answerNotes.GEAR: Gears transmit rotation through contacting teeth. Different gear sizes can alter the rate of motion.
answerNotes.HAND: A hand indicates a value on a dial. A digital display uses numerals without moving pointers.
answerNotes.MINUTE: A minute contains sixty seconds. It is a duration whether measured by a mechanical or an electronic device.

title: Inside a Vacuum Cleaner
description: Identify the parts that move air, collect dust, and make a household vacuum cleaner easier to use.
cardDescription: Identify the parts that move air, collect dust, and make a household vacuum cleaner easier to use.
focus: Different machines collect debris in bags or bins, but airflow and suction connect their main functions. The clues separate a collecting container, a cleaning attachment, and the motor producing the motion.
solvingTip: Use the function of each part. A storage space is different from a cleaning head or a flexible connection.
words: SUCTION
Drawing action caused by lower air pressure in a vacuum cleaner
FILTER
Component that traps particles as air passes through it
NOZZLE
Cleaning attachment at the working end of a vacuum hose
MOTOR
Powered component driving a vacuum cleaner's fan
BIN
Rigid dirt-collecting container in a bagless vacuum
VACUUM
First word in the name of a common powered floor cleaner
HOSE
Flexible tube connecting a vacuum body to an attachment
BRUSH
Bristled part that helps loosen debris at the cleaning head
BAG
Replaceable dirt collector in some vacuum models
DUST
Fine household particles drawn into the cleaner
CORD
Electrical cable supplying a plug-in vacuum
WHEEL
Round support allowing a vacuum body to roll
HANDLE
Part gripped when pushing an upright cleaner
SWITCH
Control used to turn a vacuum on or off

answerNotes.SUCTION: A vacuum cleaner uses a pressure difference to move air and debris. Suction is the familiar name for that drawing action.
answerNotes.FILTER: A filter is in the airflow path. It is different from a nozzle that directs air into the machine.
answerNotes.NOZZLE: A nozzle helps direct incoming airflow. Its shape depends on the surface or space the attachment is intended to reach.
answerNotes.MOTOR: The motor supplies motion to the fan or other mechanisms. The collected dirt is stored elsewhere.
answerNotes.BIN: Some machines use a bin and others use a bag. The clue specifies the bagless design.
